text: Journal of Psychotherapy Integration, Vol. 9, No. 1, 1999 Resistance as a Problem for Practice and Theory Paul L. Wachtel 1,2 "Resistance" is one of the most problematic and potentially counterproduc- tive concepts in the entire field of psychotherapy. It is at the same time one of the most crucial, pointing toward perhaps the single most important factor—or, more accurately, set of factors—in determining the success or failure of the therapeutic enterprise. Drawing on the articles by Davis and Hollon, Prochaska and Prochaska, Reid, and Eagle in this issue, as well as on the author's own perspective, this paper explores this seeming contradiction in order to point toward an integrative resolution of the differing perspectives on resistance and related phenomena. KEY WORDS: resistance; psychotherapy practice; psychotherapy theory. INTRODUCTION "Resistance" is one of the most problematic and potentially counter- productive concepts in the entire field of psychotherapy. It is at the same time one of the most crucial, pointing toward perhaps the single most important factor—or, more accurately, set of factors—in determining the success or failure of the therapeutic enterprise. These two statements may seem at first to be contradictory, but as I shall elaborate below, the contra- diction is more apparent than real. Therapists of virtually all orientations report phenomena that can easily be recognized as belonging to this general domain (see, for example, Wach- tel, 1982, as well as the papers by Davis and Hollon, Prochaska and Pro- chaska, Reid, and Eagle in this issue). All therapists find that their patients behave in ways that, at least in the short run, seem to impede the progress of the therapy and that, on inspection, reflect the manifestation in the 1City College and CUNY Graduate Center, City University of New York. 2Correspondence should be directed to Paul L. Wachtel, Department of Psychology, City College of CUNY, New York, NY 10031. 103 1053-0479/99/0300-0103$16.00/0 © 1999 Plenum Publishing Corporation therapy itself of the same anxieties, character traits, and problematic behav- ior patterns that have brought the person into therapy to begin with. And good therapists of all orientations recognize that to "blame" the patient for these characteristics is inappropriate and counterproductive. The patient is not so much "resisting" the therapist's efforts as trying to hold on for dear life to whatever safety and stability he has achieved in his life. Or, from another perspective, the patient is simply "being himself," which is, of course, precisely what the therapist wants and expects him to be. 3 Part of the challenge in conceptualizing resistance lies in this latter observation. As therapists, we want the patient to share with us the full, painful, and sometimes shameful reality of who he is and how he operates in the world. We want him to reveal to us even—or perhaps especially—those things he generally hides from other people. Indeed, we want him to reveal to us as well (again perhaps especially) those things he hides even from himself. Without the patient's doing this, our knowledge of him is likely to be superficial or at best hypothetical and abstract; there is no substitute for direct experience and direct observation. But the behavior patterns that create problems for him in his life are likely to create problems for him in the therapy as well, and thus the very characteristics we are (or should be) most eager to see are also the characteristics that are prone to frustrate our efforts. Ultimately, that frustration itself is a crucial part of the process. Often, it is only in working through quite directly how the patient thwarts his own interests that real progress is made. Evading the resistance is decidedly beside the point. This is most clear in psychoanalytic work, but it is true in other ap- proaches as well. Thus, Davis and Hollon (this issue), discussing cognitive therapy, note that "instances in which a client can't ... or won't . . . complete an assignment are typically turned into opportunities to identify and explore the client's underlying beliefs and attitudes. These instances often prove particularly instructive; the very beliefs that interfere with the process of therapy are often similar in nature to the kinds of attitudes and values that complicate the pursuit of larger life goals" (p. 42). Davis and Hollon note the parallels between this orientation on the part of cognitive therapists and the ways that psychodynamic therapists utilize the experience of difficulties arising in the therapeutic relationship to explore more general maladaptive relationship patterns in the patient's life. But it is important to be attentive to the differences as well. One 3For purposes of clarity, I shall use the male pronouns "he" or "his" when referring in generic terms to "the patient," and the female pronouns "she" and "her" when referring in generic terms to "the therapist." Wachtel104 important difference is that cognitive therapists do not assume that resis- tance is as universal as is assumed by psychoanalysis. Davis and Hollon, for example, describe four broad lines of explanation that account for clients failing to follow through on the therapeutic recommendations of cognitive therapists, and relate only one of them—problematic client atti- tudes and beliefs—to traditional psychodynamic conceptions of resistance. Cognitive therapy, they state, "is distinct from more conventional dynamic therapies in that it does not presume that such processes are universal or that their resolution should always be the primary working vehicle of change" (p. 52). This distinction may be a bit exaggerated, because psychoanalytic un- derstanding of resistance often includes the other considerations that Davis and Hollon list as separate factors influencing therapeutic failure. But it is certainly true at the very least that working with the resistances per se is seen as more central to psychoanalysis than to cognitive therapy. In that sense, ironically, resistance is more purely seen as resistance by cognitive therapists than by psychoanalysts. To be sure, as noted above, cognitive therapists too utilize the resistance at times to help the person come to terms with what he does elsewhere as well. But this activity does not have the centrality (or universality, as Davis and Hollon put it) that it does for psychoanalysis. "THEORY" OFTEN DOES NOT REPRESENT THE REALITIES OF CLINICAL PRACTICE Sometimes the differences—and the similarities—between approaches are not all that easy to determine. Both cognitive therapy and psychoanaly- sis, for example, are often depicted in overly verbal and cognitive ways that, for each, obscure the much larger range of influences that are usually essential for significant therapeutic change. Thus, Davis and Hollon, in a fairly standard depiction of cognitive therapy, state, "In cognitive therapy, the client is taught to systematically evaluate the accuracy and utility of his or her beliefs and interpretations, with the expectation that producing change in those interpretations can relieve distress and facilitate adaptive responding" (p. 35). Such a highly intellectualized account of the process of change has parallels with those descriptions of psychoanalysis that place preponderant emphasis on insight. In each instance, the therapist who takes this emphasis on the representations inside the person's head too literally is likely to have limited success. Davis and Hollon note, for example, that although cognitive therapy "center[s]" on thoughts and assumptions (p. 35), in fact cognitive therapy Resistance as a Problem 105 often includes more strictly behavioral strategies, affectively evocative tech- niques, and historical reconstruction. Demonstrating that it is the "cogni- tive" aspect of purportedly cognitive therapy that is crucial is a difficult case to make. In parallel fashion, the argument that it is "insight" that is the crucial element in a well-conducted psychoanalytic therapy, although it still has some proponents, sounds increasingly quaint. Eagle (this issue) points out clearly the much wider range of therapeuic factors that are considered important in contemporary psychoanalytic thought, noting that even the once taboo notion of the "corrective emotional experience" has reentered the psychoanalytic mainstream (see also Wachtel & DeMichele, 1998). 4 The "official" version of both cognitive and psychoanalytic therapy may appear more arid and intellectualized than these approaches are in the hands of skillful and experienced practitioners. (It is my own view that the more purely "cognitive" that either approach is in practice, the less helpful it is to patients or clients.) Eagle's account, however, does highlight what I believe is a generally greater emphasis on the affective dimension among psychoanalysts. In his depiction of resistance, it is most centrally the person's fear that change will bring danger or disruption that lies at the heart of resistance, not faulty ideas. To be sure, the conceptualization of Weiss and Sampson, which Eagle highly values (see also Eagle, 1992), places considerable emphasis on faulty beliefs, but they are viewed as more affectively rooted, and the affective dimension is more palpable, than it tends to be in cognitive therapy. RESISTANCE AND THE THERAPEUTIC RELATIONSHIP Although I have just noted that resistance (or some such phenome- non—see below regarding problems with this term) is a pervasive phenomenon in virtually all forms of psychotherapy, and even that it can be a very useful phenomenon for the therapeutic effort if properly understood and worked with, it is nonetheless the case that resistance can indeed be an impediment and that skillful therapeutic practice induces less resistance than less skilled practice. What one might label as "surplus" resistance is often the product of the therapist's overly 4As Eagle notes, the contemporary versions of this concept have been shorn of the putatively authoritarian or manipulative quality that was perceived by many in the psychoanalytic community as implicit in Alexander and French's (1946) approach. Indeed, although the basic idea of the corrective emotional experience is pervasive in the work of Kohut and his followers, of Weiss and Sampson and the Mt. Zion group, and of many object relations theorists, few actually dare speak its name. Eagle is noteworthy among psychoanalytic writers in his willingness to be explicit in referring to this idea. Wachtel106 rigid or mechanical application of a set of rules learned as the badge of belonging for a particular therapeutic orientation. As several of the authors in this series have noted, attention to the therapeutic relationship is a crucial factor in minimizing the kinds of resis- tance that hamper therapeutic progress. Davis and Hollon make the inter- esting point that clients in cognitive therapy are "in essence, being asked to suspend belief in [their] existing self-concept or worldview" (p. 36) and thus that participation in cognitive therapy often requires a "leap of faith." Davis and Hollon note as well, following Safran and Segal (1990), that "cognitive therapy is inseparable from the interpersonal context in which it is delivered" (p. 36). Thus, establishing a relationship in which the patient or client has sufficient trust in the therapist to make that leap of faith, at least on a trial basis, is a crucial part of successful therapy. From a different vantage point, Eagle similarly points to the crucial role of the therapeutic relationship. He notes that increased resistance can be a sign that the patient feels unsafe, and that such feelings of danger can derive from the ways that the therapist unwittingly communicates dispar- agement or structures the relationship in ways that are aversive or threaten- ing (cf. Wachtel, 1993). Eagle notes the research findings linking good therapeutic outcome to the quality of the therapeutic alliance, and suggests that "no matter how accurate or clever the therapist's interpretations may be, if the patient does not experience the therapist as helpful and supportive and as engaged with him or her in a joint effort, change is not likely to occur" (p. 29; again, cf. Wachtel, 1993). Put differently, the quality of the therapeutic relationship is a crucial determinant of the degree of resistance that is generated. Again, using the relationship—and attending to the quality of the relationship—is not unique to psychoanalysis. We have already noted such considerations in cognitive therapy. We may further add here another example from Davis and Hollon: In the case of the man who feared being embarrassed on job interviews, the therapist enabled him to open up when the therapist expressed puzzlement and frustration. Davis and Hollon's account emphasizes an element of modeling—"the therapist's own ability to admit failure without regarding it as a threat to his self-esteem facilitated the client's own self-disclosure" (p. 40). One can note as well, however, a number of dimensions to this intervention that illustrate the impact of the therapeutic relationship, including what systemic and strategic therapists refer to as the "one-down position." As with the mice in the research discussed by Prochaska and Prochaska, people don't like to be forced to do something. When the therapist took the position that he was helpless to make the client open up to him, the client then felt more able to choose to do so. Resistance as a Problem 107 It is useful to note, in this regard, that the original formulation of the resistance concept by Freud occurred in a context (see below) in which Freud was trying to wrest from the patient memories and desires that the patient was seen as trying to hide. Over time, Freud's understanding, and that of other analysts, became more sophisticated and, as Eagle points out, the primary vector shifted from a view of the patient as in certain ways recalcitrant and stubborn to a view that emphasized his fear of what might emerge. The more demeaning—and implicitly coercive—view remained in many analytic formulations, however, likely increasing the degree of resistance that analysts saw. The view of Dewald, for example, which Eagle quotes, portrays the patient as seeking gratification of infantile wishes, being reluctant to give up attempts to relive the past, and as reluctant to "accept. . . what is age-appropriate" (p. 7). Such a view is likely to result in a therapeutic relationship that, subtly or grossly, attempts to wrestle with the patient to force this infantile, recalcitrant child to grow up and partici- pate more maturely and appropriately in the therapy. Rather than going with the resistance—which includes validating the patient's defensive efforts even as the therapist skillfully helps the patient to relinquish them—this orientation is more likely to go against the resistance, and thereby to in- crease it (cf. Wachtel, 1993). There is no one appropriate stance with regard to resistance, as there is no one appropriate stance in clinical work in general. As Weiss (1998) has noted, discussing work approached from the orientation of his joint work with Sampson, in working with patients who "suffer primarily from the belief that they have no right either to have their own opinions or to question the opinions of authorities," it is important that the therapist particularly refrain from expressing her own opinion too insistently and that she encourage the patient's own judgments on matters. He adds, how- ever, that "if patients suffer primarily from the belief that they do not deserve protection," the therapist may be more helpful by being more active and assertive, conveying to the patient that she will not be neglectful or passive as perhaps the patient's parents were. In this connection, we may contextualize Eagle's discussion of Weiss and Sampson's work and be stimulated in further ways by the example Eagle offers in illustration of that work. Eagle notes, in discussing a case in which the patient offered a gift to his analyst, that the analyst tactfully refused the gift, in part because it violated the analytic contract. But Weiss's perspective, noted above, implicitly raises a question about that very con- tract. For some patients, it may feel securely protective and, as Eagle suggests, a sign that the analyst would not be easily seduced. But as Eagle notes, there is more than one way to understand the sequence he describes. And, however we understand this particular case, there are surely cases in Wachtel108 which the patient's predominant childhood experience was of parents who hewed rigidly to strict rules or who could not accept that their child had something useful to offer them. In such cases, even tactful refusal of an offer of a gift may constitute "failing" rather than "passing" the test, whereas reflective acceptance of the gift—assuming it is not so large or significant that it creates a genuine conflict of interest or ethical breach— may be therapeutic and healing. Skillful attention to the nuances of the therapeutic relationship, and how it might constitute either a continuation or a disconfirmation of the problematic patterns established earlier in the patient's life, can go a long way toward diminishing the "surplus resistance" that can sink the therapeutic effort. "RESISTANCE" AND VALUES Psychotherapy is not a value-free enterprise. As a consequence, determining just what constitutes resistance can be less straightforward than many discussions seem to imply. An operational definition that resistance is what the therapist sees as resistance or calls resistance might satisfy those who—as with "intelligence is what intelligence tests measure"—are soothed by such pseudo-scientific mumbo-jumbo; but it does little to enable us to gain much of a foothold on what really is in the patient's interest. Was the readiness of Reid's Navajo patient to accommodate to the expectations of his friends and his tribal traditions a lack of assertiveness, and was his reluctance to take on Reid's urbanized value system a reflection of resistance? Or as Reid suggests in reflecting on the case, was this an instance of a therapist selling his own value system and failing to be respect- ful of and attentive to what mattered most to the patient? The answer to such a question is not context free. The therapist's aims and values will shape how she sees such dilemmas, which on some scale develop in virtually all therapies. Other examples offered by Reid highlight still other dimensions of the potential clash of cultural values and assumptions, and of the ways in which resistance can, in essence, be constructed as a phenomenon by the therapist's interpretation of what is transpiring. There can be many reasons beside the one Reid offers—"she is used to doing a number of things simultane- ously" (p. 59)—for a Native American mother to bring her children into a therapy session. But what is most important in the present context is that not only may the therapist's and the patient's construction of the event differ significantly, but the therapist's wish that she not bring the baby may seem decidedly odd to the patient—and to her community as well. Resistance as a Problem 109 Similar clashes of perceptions of what is right and normal can occur between patients and their parents as well as therapists. Reid notes, for example, the ways in which parents who hold more traditional values may differ from their children whose values are more individualistic and less defined by a family or "Collateral" focus. Actually, the three examples I have cited from Reid are not unrelated. They all reflect choices regarding a rather fundamental dilemma in human life generally, and especially one experienced by people caught between more traditional cultures and the highly individualized culture of the United States and Western Europe. This dilemma or conflict has been discussed, among others, by Fromm (1941) in terms of individuation vs. aloneness, by Bakan (1966) in terms of agency vs. communion and the "duality of human existence," and by Blatt (1990) in terms of interpersonal relatedness and self-definition. Modern industrialized cul- tures tend to emphasize the more differentiating end of each duality, highlighting autonomy and what in psychoanalytic terms is referred to as separation-individuation. Although therapists probably tend to have higher regard for relatedness than the American population at large (especially than the population of successful upper middle class individu- als), they are nonetheless usually products of the highly individualistic culture that the United States shares with other modern industrialized societies. As a consequence, they are likely to harbor values that empha- size growing away from the context of the family in various ways and differentiating oneself from the embedding matrix of the culture at large (cf. Wachtel, 1983, in press). Their emphasis on relatedness is more likely to be on a kind of voluntary relatedness more associated with friends (and, in our divorce-prone society, with spouses) than with family, especially extended family. Other cultures, however—and people in our own culture closer to more traditional values—order the keys to the good life in quite different fashion. Apropos Eagle's discussion (p. 12) of patients' pathogenic beliefs that separating from one's parents and leading an independent life is tantamount to seriously harming or destroy- ing them, it is essential to be aware that in certain cultures and subcultures it is experienced by parents as cruel and hurtful if their children separate to the degree that is common—and regarded as healthy—in American society. Reid emphasizes that consonance between the patient's and therapist's implicit value systems and ways of constructing the world may be a signifi- cant factor in determining the degree of resistance that is manifested in the therapy. More than whether the therapist is "psychoanalytic" or "cognitive- behavioral" or whatever, the crucial factor may be whether the patient experiences the therapist as someone who sees the world as he does, or at Wachtel110 the very least, someone who understands and respects the way the patient sees the world. Value issues arise not just in terms of cultural differences. Strong value presumptions can enter in even in work with people from the same culture or subculture, and they can at times be rather subtle. Thus, for example, I quite thoroughly share Prochaska and Prochaska's views about smoking, but would nonetheless note that the term "precontemplative," when applied to a smoker who has decided that the pleasure he or she receives is worth more than the risk, is not a value-neutral phrase. Since it implies that that person is stuck for the moment in an early, unenlightened stage, the term can be experienced as demeaning and as an expression of the authors' values cloaked in scientific terminology. One may reconnect this issue to the dimension of culture discussed by Reid by noting that that many Europe- ans and South Americans view American culture as excessively risk avoid- ant to the point of making life less interesting and pleasurable, and that they see as puritanical or as an expression of an intrusive nanny-state the laws in many American cities restricting smoking in restaurants and other public spaces. Again, my own values line up much more closely with what I take to be Prochaska and Prochaska's; but that does not prevent me from being a bit uneasy about the value element inherent in the phrase ' 'precontemplative.'' To be sure, the scheme Prochaska and Prochaska introduce is one that is oriented toward regularities they have observed empirically in the temporal sequencing of change, and their overall stages of change model has been an interesting and important contribution. Applied specifically to people who are seeking change—but who approach the prospect ambiva- lently, with multiple rationalizations in the early stage of the process—their terminology is less problematic. Even less problematic still is the employ- ment of the term "precontemplative" retrospectively, from the vantage point of how a person now actively engaged in the change process, or having already changed, had viewed matters much earlier. But it is very easy for there to be slippage and for such terms to be applied to people who are not seeking change (and who are labeled as precontemplative for that very reason) or to people who do not view themselves either as lacking in sufficient contemplation or as pre-anything, but as people who have finished contemplating and made a decision that is simply different from the decision that Prochaska and Prochaska—or I—would make. When Prochaska and Prochaska state that "while most people in our society tend to judge the hazards of smoking as clearly outweighing the benefits, smokers in the precontemplation stage report the opposite pat- tern" (p. 90), could we not as readily say that people who judge the benefits as outweighing the hazards are, by definition, labeled as precontemplators? Resistance as a Problem 111 And does that not strip the concept of some of its empirical content and reveal a hidden value structure underneath? (Again, it is a value structure I share, and I do not mean to overlook the substantial empirical content in their overall approach to stages of change. I simply want to highlight the easy slippage when we utilize terminology that conflates empirical and value considerations.) It is worth noting as well another terminological choice in the labeling of the "contemplation" stage. Such a term is unlikely to be noteworthy to therapists whose "home" orientation is cognitive-behavioral, but for me it evokes the same concern about an overly cognitive/intellectual view of the therapeutic process that I discussed earlier. An alternative label, centered on a quality that Prochaska and Prochaska describe as characteristic of this stage, might be to call it the stage of "ambivalence." In one sense, such a labeling adds little empirical content. I suggest this term as an alternative, after all, based on Prochaska and Prochaska's own description of the ambivalence that is characteristic of this stage. Nor is my point that the term "ambivalence" is "better." There is certainly plenty of baggage associated with the term "ambivalence," and in high- lighting the baggage associated with contemplation, my aim is not to offer a ranking. Indeed, the term "ambivalence" has often been associated with an orientation that rejects any kind of activism in psychotherapy and, by highlighting that there are always (at least) two sides to the patient's feel- ings, has provided a convenient rationale for not being active. 5 In contrast, one of the strengths of Prochaska and Prochaska's approach, in my view, is their active and structured approach to change. Especially for the kinds of focused and clearly defined problems primarily discussed in their paper, such structure and activism is very useful. Nonetheless, as noted above, I regard an overly cognitive and intellectualized conceptualization of the change process as a problem broadly evident in orientations from psycho- analysis to cognitive therapy. And although Prochaska and Prochaska's own approach includes considerably more than purely cognitive features, the degree to which overly cognitive or rationalistic thinking and terminol- ogy have gained common usage in our literature makes me want to call attention to the particular terms they have chosen to employ. 5In highlighting this potentially impeding use of the concept, I am not minimizing its utility. I offer it as an alternative descriptive hook for the stage of change Prochaska and Prochaska call contemplative because I do believe that ambivalence is an extraordinarily useful concept. The ways in which observations about ambivalence can be used to oppose therapeutic activism are contingent, not essential. Elsewhere (Wachtel, 1993) I have discussed how attention to the patient's ambivalence can lead in quite different directions from those that have tradition- ally been stressed in psychoanalytic accounts of therapy. Wachtel112 FURTHER COMMENTS ON RESISTANCE AND STAGES OF CHANGE Prochaska and Prochaska make an important point in emphasizing the diversity of processes that combine in a successful change effort, as well as in pointing out that what works at one moment in the work may not at another. Their stage-oriented transtheoretical approach highlights both the useful contributions that different orientations make and the ways in which their methods may be misapplied if, for example, potentially effective be- havioral interventions are undertaken without sufficient preparation or important clarifications deriving from psychoanalytic exploration are not followed up at a later stage with other interventions that encourage action. In this, they make a valuable contribution to psychotherapy integration. But it is important to point out that, in complex clinical cases, the patient may be at different "stages" with regard to different issues at the same time. Examples drawn from relatively single-focus change efforts such as stopping smoking may obscure this complexity, creating a picture of a smoother and more monotonic set of stages than I think it is their intention to convey. This is an important issue to keep in mind because a good deal of the contentiousness between orientations that the psychotherapy integration movement developed in order to address derives from therapists of different orientations having as their point of reference quite different kinds of cases or quite different goals in the nature of the work they do. Failure to see the contribution of alternative approaches derives in part from the false assumption that therapists of other orientations are seeing the same kinds of cases and/or pursuing the same therapeutic goals. Often, this is simply not the case. IS "RESISTANCE" THE RIGHT TERM? I have used the term "resistance" throughout most of this paper be- cause it is so standard a term in the field and hence a useful shorthand for referring to the phenomena I wished to address. It was also a useful term in this context because it was used by the other authors in this series (largely for similar reasons). But it remains to discuss the term itself, because I believe that in fact it is a poor term, no matter how venerable it has become. The term "resistance" was introduced by Freud at a very early stage in the history of psychoanalysis, and its formulation, I suggest, reflected the convergence of several considerations at once. To begin with, Freud from the beginning conceptualized the therapeutic process in such a way that it was virtually coterminous with his research aim. That is, it was Resistance as a Problem 113 discovery that would be curative in his view, an assumption that was very convenient for a researcher whose research subjects were also his patients. Freud was very explicit in his more autobiographical writings that he lacked what he called therapeutic zeal. He aimed to be remembered most of all as a discoverer. Blockages in the patient's associations, premature termina- tion of the therapy, missed sessions, etc., were therefore not only impedi- ments to the therapeutic process but to Freud's interest in finding out what was hidden in the recesses of the patient's unconscious. Resistance, therefore, had from the beginning a double-edged quality that different therapists or different readers of the psychoanalytic literature could interpret differently. On the one hand, the notion of resistance could be read—and accurately read—as a wise and humane concept that pointed to the painful reality that the same anxieties and other difficulties that plagued the patient in his life generally were likely to show up in the therapy. It could alert the therapist to this likelihood, enabling her to be more sophisticated and effective in her efforts to help the patient and, in particular, to use their occurrence in the therapy room to the advantage of the therapeutic effort. Eagle highlights usefully and authoritatively this (one might say) progressive conceptualization of resistance, and Davis and Hollon describe how it has been usefully assimilated even by cognitive and cognitive-behavioral therapists. On the other hand, the parentage of the concept and the term includes, I believe, Freud's own interests, which did not always coincide with those of the patient as thoroughly as he liked to believe (Wachtel, 1987, Chapter 12). That is, Freud's experience, I suggest, was often of the patient resisting his efforts to make discoveries. The damn patient wouldn't come across with the goods! Those who see the concept of resistance as simply blaming the patient, placing the locus of any lack of progress in the therapy on the patient's recalcitrance, miss (whether for reasons of ideology or narrowness of vision) the more humane and sophisticated aspects of the concept depicted by Eagle and many others. But they are not distorting in a vacuum, as it were. There is such a thread woven into the concept of resistance, a thread that was inserted into the fabric of the concept at the very origins of psychoanalytic therapy and investigation and that, I believe, continues to be evident not infrequently in the ways that analysts talk about their patients. It can be said—and I would be the first to say so—that when resistance is understood in such a demeaning or adversarial way (with the patient viewed as recalcitrant, infantile, manipulative, trying to extract forbidden gratifica- tions, etc.—cf. Wile, 1984), this is a miscarriage of the concept, a faulty way of conceptualizing and thinking about resistance. But it is not a mistake that has no foundation in the history of psychoanalytic thought and practice. Wachtel114 The varied meanings of resistance lead to ambiguities that are at once evocative and hard to assign a really clear meaning. Thus Eagle (p. 15) refers to mental representations that are "highly resistant to change." What exactly does resistant to change mean here? One may call to mind the classic Henny Youngman line in which, asked the question "How is your wife?," Youngman would respond, "compared to what?" In saying that certain representations are highly resistant to change, we can similarly ask, Compared to what? That is, is the assumption that there is something inherently or "internally" sticky about those representations? Is there something in the way they are coded and laid down in the nervous system that renders them less responsive to new experiences that might alter them? Or, alternatively, is what makes them seem more "resistant" to change that they are closely linked to interpersonal action sequences in which their effect is to evoke behavior that recreates the same experience again? (cf. Wachtel, 1981,1997) In the latter case, the representation itself may be no more resistant to change than any other representation, but merely less likely to actually be confronted with new, potentially disconfirming experi- ences that could activate their potential for change or accommodation. 6 Eagle notes, for example, that part of how early mental representations are maintained with little change over the years is that they repeatedly lead us to "form and transform relationships so that they conform to our early acquired expectations and schemas. One of the primary ways that we do this is to behave in particular ways that will elicit just those responses from the other that will tend to perpetuate early relationship patterns." (p. 15, emphasis in original; cf. Wachtel, 1993, 1997). RESISTANCE AND VARIATIONS IN THERAPEUTIC COMMUNICATION When the concept of resistance is used problematically, the variance is essentially attributed almost exclusively to the patient. It is the patient who is resistant. More satisfactory conceptualizations of resistance attri- bute much of the variance to the therapist and/or to her techniques. From such a vantage point, resistance is at the very least a product of the dyad rather than the patient alone. The therapist, from this viewpoint, 6Please note the question marks and "maybe's" in the foregoing sentences. I am not asserting that an absence of difference in the malleability of the representations themselves isnecessarily the case, but rather raising an alternative understanding that cannot be ruled out by most of the observations that seem to imply greater "resistance" to change. Stated differently, I am offering an alternative explanation of why they may be more resistant to change. It is likely that almost all representations have a certain degree of "stickiness." Neither assimilation nor accommodation are typically totalistic phenomena (cf. Wachtel, 1981). Resistance as a Problem 115 bears a greater burden of responsibility, but also has more opportunity to use her skills to reduce resistance, or at least to reduce surplus resistance (see above). Much of my own work in recent years has been especially concerned with precisely this aim of reducing surplus resistance. Eagle notes that the cues the therapist gives out can make a substantial difference in the kind and degree of resistance that is encountered. Some of those cues are uncon- scious, a product of the therapist's conflicts or her countertransference. But much of what we convey to the patient is in our conscious control and can be presented in more effectively therapeutic ways if we are alert to the numerous dimensions and subtleties of our communications to the patient (Wachtel, 1993). Prochaska and Prochaska's reframing of relapse as an opportunity rather than just a setback—a measure that has data backing up its utility—is a good example of the kinds of therapeutic strategies or modes of communication to which I am alluding. On the other hand, Davis and Hollon's reframing of the psychoanalytic notion of infantile motivations into "dysfunctional beliefs" (p. 41) seems to me less adequate. Saying to someone "you're not infantile, you're just dysfunctional" is unlikely to be especially heartwarming a message, notwithstanding the brief emotional lift the first few words might generate until the rest of the sentence is heard. (Compare in this regard Wile's [1984] discussion of similarly thin improvements in some of Kohut's reformulations of standard psychoana- lytic conceptualizations.) Ultimately, good therapeutic work converges on a view of the phenom- ena of resistance that is held by therapists of many perspectives but is easily lost by all as well. It is very largely in the tension between pejorative and empathic readings of the patient's behavior that success or failure is determined. The problematic formulation by Davis and Hollon just noted, for example, can be contrasted with their statement, shortly after, that even when there appears what they call "active resistance," what constrains the patient from taking appropriate and helpful action is "typically nothing more than a reasonable desire to avoid some consequence of action that most people would consider undesirable" (p. 42). Here, their view con- verges strongly with the view of Wile that I just cited as an implicit critique of their conceptualization, as well as with much of Eagle's paper and with important aspects of Reid's and of Prochaska and Prochaska's. Psychotherapeutic work is among the most rewarding and most frustrating endeavors known to man. The phenomena traditionally labeled as resistance can be a medium for both experiences. It is in under- standing so-called resistance in more salutary and humane ways that the frustration can be reduced and the rewards (for patient and therapist alike) expanded. 116 Wachtel REFERENCES Alexander, F., & French, T.
